passage: I'm Raghav, and I was in the lab when Divyansh realised the results table had the wrong units. The group report was due in two days. Divyansh went quiet, checked twice, then walked straight to our lab professor. "I entered the readings in the wrong units in the table, so the graphs built from it are off. I can redo them by tomorrow evening. Should I also tell you what else it affects?" The professor was silent a moment, then said, "Thank you for telling me now, not on Friday. Send me the redo tomorrow." Divyansh looked pale but steady. The rest of us had privately wondered whether to keep quiet. The next evening the corrected report was in the professor's inbox.

qa.q: What had Divyansh got wrong in the results table?
qa.a: Divyansh had entered the readings in the wrong units.

qa.q: What was Divyansh probably feeling while telling the professor?
qa.a: Nervous but steady, looking pale yet willing to take responsibility.

qa.q: What made Divyansh's way of owning the mistake effective?
qa.a: Divyansh spoke early, said exactly what happened and offered a redo by the next evening.

qa.q: How did the professor react to hearing about the error now rather than on Friday?
qa.a: The professor thanked Divyansh and accepted the redo, valuing the early warning.

grounding: Shows a young adult telling a professor about a mistake early, saying what happened and what will be done.

passage:
Monday. On a bus after class, Uma realised she had sent the tournament registration to the wrong email address. The deadline was Friday. That evening she messaged the captain, Francis: "I made a mistake. I sent the form to the wrong address. I'll resend it and phone the organisers tomorrow." Francis replied, "Thanks for telling me tonight."

Tuesday. Uma resent the form at eight and phoned the organisers, who confirmed that the right one had arrived.

Thursday. At practice Francis told the team the entry was confirmed and that Uma had caught it in time. Uma's face went warm, but she had the confirmation email ready to show.

qa.q: What did Uma get wrong with the registration?
qa.a: Uma sent the tournament registration to the wrong email address.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she messaged the captain that evening?
qa.a: Anxious and embarrassed, but ready to take responsibility.

qa.q: Which steps limited the damage?
qa.a: Uma told Francis the same evening, resent the form and phoned the organisers to confirm it had arrived.

qa.q: How might Francis have felt on receiving the message that evening?
qa.a: Probably concerned but appreciative, since Francis thanked Uma for saying it that night.

grounding: Shows a young adult owning a mistake quickly to a teammate, saying what happened and what will be done.

passage:
Yusuf, you broke your friend's camera and you're scared to tell him? Sit. Your Gurleen phuphi will tell you about my third year of college.
Our group had spent two months collecting survey data for Professor Bhalla. One night, cleaning up the shared folder, I deleted the master file. No backup. I sat there looking at the screen, cold all over.
I could have said nothing. Someone else had access too. But by eight the next morning I was outside the professor's cabin. My voice shook. "Sir, I deleted the master file last night. It was my mistake. I have the raw forms, and I'll re-enter them by Friday. I've asked two friends to help."
He was quiet, then said, "Thank you for telling me first." We finished on Thursday.
At the end of the year he wrote my recommendation letter. He mentioned that morning in it.

qa.q: By when did Gurleen promise to re-enter the data?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: How did young Gurleen feel after deleting the file?
qa.a: Gurleen felt cold all over, frightened and ashamed, tempted for a moment to stay silent.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Going to the professor first thing in the morning, saying what happened and what the fix would be, before anyone else found out.

qa.q: How did Professor Bhalla see Gurleen's confession?
qa.a: He respected it, thanking her for telling him first and later mentioning that morning in her recommendation letter.

grounding: An elder recalls owning a serious mistake early to a professor, with a plan to fix it, and earning respect.

passage:
The class demo was at eleven. At 10:25, Wasim, the second-year student helping in the chemistry lab, realised he had made the copper sulphate solution ten times too strong. He had read the wrong line on the sheet.
His first thought was to hope nobody noticed. His second was the thirty first-year students who would record wrong results.
He found Dr Nazia in the prep room. "Ma'am, I made a mistake. The solution is ten times too strong. I read the wrong line. I can make a fresh batch in fifteen minutes if you can start with the theory part."
Dr Nazia looked at the clock, then at him. "Go. I'll talk for fifteen."
His hands were not quite steady as he measured, but he checked each number twice. The new solution was ready at 10:52.
After class, Dr Nazia said, "Most people hide that. You didn't. That's why I trust you with the lab."

qa.q: How much too strong was the solution?
qa.a: Ten times too strong.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel as he remade the solution?
qa.a: Wasim was nervous, his hands not quite steady, but determined to get it right, checking each number twice.

qa.q: What made Wasim's way of owning the mistake effective?
qa.a: He told Dr Nazia at once, said exactly what went wrong and offered a specific fix with a time, so the damage was contained.

qa.q: How does Dr Nazia see Wasim after the class?
qa.a: Dr Nazia trusts him more, saying most people hide such mistakes and he didn't.

grounding: Shows a young adult who reports his lab mistake immediately with a clear fix, limiting the damage and earning trust.

passage:
Yogesh, an intern at a small education NGO in Dadar, pressed "send" on the monthly donor newsletter at 4:02. At 4:09 a reply came from a donor: "The donate button takes me to last year's page."
Yogesh's stomach dropped. Eight hundred people. He checked: yes, he had copied the old link.
He could quietly fix the web page and hope. Instead he walked to Anand's desk. "Anand, I sent the newsletter with last year's donation link. I've already checked; the old page still works but shows the wrong campaign. I can send a short correction email in ten minutes, and I'll add a link check to our sending list."
Anand rubbed his forehead, then nodded. "Do it. Keep it short."
The correction went out at 4:25. Three donors replied, "Thanks for the update." In the team meeting on Friday, Anand used the new link check as an example for everyone.

qa.q: At what time did Yogesh send the newsletter?
How did Yogesh feel when he read the donor's reply?
qa.a: Yogesh felt a sharp drop of fear, realising eight hundred people had the wrong link.

qa.q: Which parts of Yogesh's message to Anand made it a good way to own the mistake?
qa.a: It said what happened, what he had already checked, the fix and timing, and a change to prevent it happening again.

qa.q: How does Anand respond to the news?
qa.a: Anand is briefly stressed, rubbing his forehead, but trusts Yogesh's plan and later uses the link check as a team example.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who tells his manager about a mistake early, with what happened and what he will do, limiting the damage.

passage:
"Sir, do you have five minutes? It's about the survey data."
Professor Darshan looked up from his laptop. "Come in, Rukmini."
"Last night I was cleaning the response sheet and deleted forty rows by mistake. I saved before I noticed."
"Forty out of how many?"
"Two hundred and ten. I found an older copy from Monday on the shared drive, so only Tuesday's and Wednesday's responses are gone. That's the forty."
"Hmm. And what do you plan to do?"
"I've already written to the class reps who circulated the form, asking those students to fill it in again. I've also turned on version history so this can't happen silently again. The analysis may be two days late. I wanted you to hear it from me first, not in the report."
He took off his glasses. "Most people tell me after the deadline. Send me the new timeline tonight."
"I will. Thank you, Sir."
As she left, he was already writing a note for the other groups: turn on version history.

qa.q: How many rows did Rukmini delete?
qa.a: Forty rows, out of two hundred and ten.

qa.q: What does Professor Darshan's reply suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels respect, even some admiration, because most people tell him after the deadline and Rukmini came early with a plan.

qa.q: Which parts of Rukmini's message made it work?
qa.a: Rukmini said exactly what happened and how much was lost, what was already being done to recover and prevent it, and the likely delay, all before the deadline.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had waited until the report was due?
qa.a: The professor would hear it late, there would be less time to collect the responses again, and trust would likely drop.

grounding: Shows a young adult telling a professor about a mistake early, with what happened and what they will do about it.
